Doeg the Edomite
DOH-eg the EE-doh-myte
n. proper (biblical figure; Saul's chief shepherd; murderer of the priests of Nob)
Hebrew Do’eg (fearful, anxious; from a root suggesting a state of dread or anxiety); Edomite designates his ethnic descent from Esau (Edom), Jacob's brother and rival. The designation “Edomite” carries loaded covenantal weight in the OT: Edom was the nation born of the rejected twin, living outside the covenant promises. David's inscription to Psalm 52 names Doeg explicitly as the occasion for that psalm's meditation on the wickedness of the powerful slanderer.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Doeg the Edomite was Saul's chief shepherd, an Edomite in the service of Israel's king, whose treachery produced one of the most appalling single acts of violence in the Old Testament narrative: the massacre of eighty-five priests of the LORD at Nob. The sequence unfolds in 1 Samuel 21–22: when David fled Saul and came to Ahimelech the priest at Nob, Doeg was present, “detained before the LORD” (1 Sam 21:7) — the reason for his detention is unspecified but his presence in a sacred context heightens the irony of what follows. He reported David's visit to Saul (1 Sam 22:9–10), triggering Saul's murderous rage against the priests he accused of treason. When Saul commanded his own servants to kill the priests and they refused, Doeg stepped forward: “And the king said to Doeg, 'You turn and kill the priests!' So Doeg the Edomite turned and struck the priests — and he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod” (1 Sam 22:18). He then destroyed Nob itself, “both men and women, children and nursing infants, and oxen and donkeys and sheep, with the edge of the sword” (1 Sam 22:19). Psalm 52, ascribed to David in response to this atrocity, meditates on the moral portrait of a man like Doeg: one who boasts in evil, whose tongue is like a sharp razor, who loves evil more than good and lying more than speaking righteousness. His fate is the fate Scripture assigns to all who use treacherous speech and violent power against the servants of God: uprooted, struck down, removed from the land of the living. He stands in Scripture as the archetype of the violent informer and the treacherous servant of a wicked king.

Webster 1828 Definition

Saul's Edomite chief shepherd who informed on David's visit to Ahimelech the priest at Nob and then single-handedly massacred eighty-five priests at Saul's command; the occasion for Psalm 52's meditation on the wicked tongue and the fate of the violent slanderer.

DOEG THE EDOMITE, n. (Heb. Do’eg ha-ʾEdōmī). Chief shepherd of Saul's livestock; an Edomite in the service of the Israelite king. His two appearances in the narrative — at Nob (1 Sam 21:7) and at Gibeah (1 Sam 22:9–19) — bracket the worst single act of priestly massacre in Israel's history.

His presence at Nob when David fled there was providentially significant for David's danger: Doeg recognized David's identity and reported it to Saul with sufficient detail to indict Ahimelech of conspiracy (1 Sam 22:9–10), though Ahimelech had acted in innocence, not knowing David was fleeing the king.

The massacre he executed at Saul's command was total: eighty-five priests wearing the linen ephod, plus the entire population of the city of Nob — men, women, children, nursing infants, livestock. It was the slaughter of a covenant city and its sacred personnel at the hands of a foreigner employed by a rejected king — the concentrated expression of Saul's apostasy in a single atrocity.

Psalm 52's inscription (“when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said to him, 'David has come to the house of Ahimelech'”) frames the psalm as David's theological response: not merely personal lament but prophetic meditation on the type of person Doeg represents and the doom Scripture pronounces on such men.

His Edomite identity is not incidental: he is the outsider, the son of the rejected line of Esau, doing the rejected king's worst work. He embodies the covenant warning that apostasy enlists pagan instruments — and that the God who keeps covenant will ultimately vindicate His servants against every Doeg.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 21:7 — "Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. And his name was Doeg, an Edomite, the chief of Saul's shepherds."

1 Samuel 22:9 — "Then answered Doeg the Edomite, who was set over the servants of Saul, and said, “I saw the son of Jesse going to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub.”"

1 Samuel 22:18 — "And the king said to Doeg, “You turn and kill the priests!” So Doeg the Edomite turned and struck the priests — and he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod."

Psalm 52:1 — "Why do you boast in evil, O mighty man? The goodness of God endures continually."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Doeg the Edomite appears in no cultural-redefinition project. The principle to recover is the biblical witness that treacherous service to a wicked ruler — using one's proximity to power to destroy the innocent — is an abomination to God that Scripture does not pass over in silence but names, records, and judges.

expand to see more

Doeg is sometimes treated in popular retellings as a minor figure of the narrative background — a functionary, almost accidental in his role. The biblical text refuses this reduction. He is named, his ethnic identity is stated, his position in Saul's household is specified, and his deed is recorded in detail that includes the count of eighty-five priests. God does not allow the names of the treacherous servants of wicked kings to fade. Psalm 52 ensures that Doeg's kind will be remembered — not as tragic bystanders but as agents of evil who chose violence when they could have refused it.

A minimalist reading reduces the Nob massacre to a power-struggle episode in Iron Age Canaan, treating it as one incident among many in the chaotic politics of early monarchy. The biblical text judges it by a different standard: eighty-five men wearing the linen ephod, the priestly garment that signified service before the LORD, were killed by a foreigner at a rejected king's command. The city of Nob — a priestly city — was annihilated. The narrative presents this not as a political miscalculation but as the fruit of Saul's apostasy, and Doeg as its willing instrument. The faithful remnant of Nob's priests, represented by Abiathar who escaped, would serve David — the anointed one Saul had tried to destroy — for the rest of his reign.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From 1 Samuel 21–22 and Psalm 52; an Edomite servant of Saul who became the instrument of the priestly massacre at Nob; his story is the dark counterpart to Abiathar's escape and David's grief over the priests he had inadvertently endangered.

expand to see more

Nob, the city of the priests — the priestly city near Jerusalem where the displaced tabernacle vessels may have resided; Ahimelech's community there served the sacred bread and the sword of Goliath; Doeg's knowledge of David's visit there was the intelligence that triggered Saul's purge.

Edomite identity — Doeg is consistently identified as “the Edomite”; his ethnic otherness underscores the irony: an Edomite, son of Esau the rejected, serves Israel's rejected king and kills Israel's priests; the chosen line destroyed by the rejected line, both now outside covenant faithfulness.

Detention before the LORD (1 Sam 21:7) — the phrase “detained before the LORD” may indicate a vow, a legal matter pending resolution, or ritual uncleanness requiring confinement; his presence in the sacred precincts at the moment of David's arrival was not accidental in the providential narrative.

Psalm 52 (Davidic inscription) — the psalm ascribed to David's response to Doeg's treachery meditates on the powerful wicked tongue and pronounces the divine verdict: God will break down the slanderer, uproot him, remove him from the land of the living, and the righteous will see and fear and laugh at the one who refused to make God his strength.

Abiathar's survival (1 Sam 22:20–23) — the one priest who escaped the massacre fled to David and reported it; David's response is notable: “I knew on that day...that he would surely tell Saul” — David takes moral responsibility for having endangered the priests while knowing Doeg was there; his grief is the counterpoint to Doeg's treachery.

Usage

"Doeg warns against the moral corruption of proximity to wicked power: he was not forced to report David's visit; he was not forced to kill the priests when Saul's own servants refused; he chose treachery and violence when he could have chosen silence or refusal."

"Psalm 52 uses Doeg's portrait as a theological type: the mighty man who boasts in evil, whose tongue is a sharp razor, who loves evil more than good — this is the archetype of the powerful slanderer in every generation, and Scripture's verdict on him is unequivocal."

"The massacre at Nob is the fulfillment of the prophecy against the house of Eli (1 Sam 2:31–33): the priestly house would be cut off; Doeg was the instrument of that judgment even as he acted from malice, which is how God exercises sovereignty through the sinful choices of sinful men without Himself becoming the author of their sin."
